03

The Split Triad

timestamp: 1:28

Here is a split triad in G major:

If we compare a regular G major triad to a G major split triad, we can see that it is the bottom two
notes that move.

Regular G Major Triad
(
Root Position
)

Split G Major Triad
(
Root Position
)

In root position, the second note of the triad moves up to the third, back down to the second, and then
down to the root. This creates a sense of movement within one chord.

Remember, in the split triad, your second finger goes on the second note of the scale. So here, your
second finger will be on A natural.

Chord Sequence

timestamp: 2:20

Now we’re going to explore several ways to incorporate this split triad into a chord sequence.
First, we need to create a chord sequence to practice with.

The chord sequence will be in the key of G major. Here is the G major scale:

05

Add The Split Triad

timestamp: 4:30 Breakdown / 7:00 Playthrough

At the end of each bar, add the split triad on G major. There are some awkward jumps here, so work
through this slowly, hands separately at first, and then bring them together.

G split triad

G split triad

G split triad

G split triad

It doesn’t matter that we’re playing the same G major triad across all the
chords—this is the
swan method
(as described in the video!)

It involves having the piano fill consistently reference the home key while
the underlying harmony shifts.

For now, don’t worry too much about
why
this works; just get used to the
sound! You’ll soon begin to recognise this technique in so many songs!

07

Mix & Match!

timestamp: 9:14 Breakdown / 11:37 Playthrough

Now it’s time to get a bit more creative. We’re going to experiment with mix and matching the split
triads in our right hand and explore the sounds we can create.

The key point here is that the split triad in the right hand doesn’t have to match the underlying chord.

For instance, over an Em7 chord, try using a D major triad. This is the first step toward developing
your own unique chord sequences that go beyond conventional chord shapes!

Looking To Take This Further?
🤔

If you're up for a challenge, create your own chord sequence in a different key and
apply some of the techniques from this Lesson Book.

Alternatively, try integrating these techniques into a song you're currently working
on.

The key takeaway is to blend the different approaches we’ve explored. Avoid sticking to the same
accompaniment over and over. By mixing up your techniques and trying new methods, your playing
will sound more natural, creative, and dynamic.
